title: Rethinking Myanmar’s Union from the periphery
gist: Five years of civil war have inverted Myanmar's federalism debate: ethnic armed groups like the Arakan Army already govern, tax and judge territory, so any settlement must share power that has emerged from the periphery rather than devolve it from Naypyidaw. ASEAN's state-centric Five-Point Consensus approach risks missing these realities.

insights.claim: In Myanmar, political authority is increasingly emerging from the periphery rather than being devolved from the centre, often without involvement of the Naypyidaw government, reversing the long-held assumption that the future order would be designed centrally.
insights.speaker: Yuyun Wahyuningrum
insights.so_what: Any investor or diplomat modelling Myanmar's political future around a single central government counterpart is working from an outdated map.
insights.quote: Increasingly, the reverse is happening: political authority is emerging from the periphery, often without Naypyidaw.

insights.claim: The Arakan Army in Rakhine and powerful ethnic organisations in Shan State and other border areas control substantial territory and run their own systems of administration, taxation, justice and security — functioning governments rather than mere autonomy demands.
insights.speaker: Yuyun Wahyuningrum
insights.so_what: De facto local authorities control taxation and security in resource and trade corridors, meaning access to those areas runs through non-state actors.
insights.quote: These are not simply demands for future autonomy. They are forms of government already operating on the ground.

insights.claim: Myanmar is not undergoing a single political transition: political authority is consolidating at local and state level in some ethnic borderlands, while in Bamar-majority Anyar resistance remains fragmented and civilians face intense military violence.
insights.speaker: Yuyun Wahyuningrum
insights.so_what: Risk and governance conditions vary sharply by region, so country-level assessments of Myanmar obscure more than they reveal.

insights.claim: Myanmar may not be moving from federalism to confederation so much as remaking federalism from the ground up.
insights.speaker: Yuyun Wahyuningrum
insights.so_what: Points to a likely settlement with asymmetric autonomy rather than either a centralised state or outright break-up.

insights.so_what: The junta continues to rely on intensive force, underscoring that no near-term peace dividend should be assumed.

insights.claim: The March 2026 creation of the Steering Council for the Emergence of a Federal Democratic Union (SCEF) shows resistance actors remain committed to a federal union while reflecting the growing weight of states and ethnic resistance organisations in shaping Myanmar's future.
insights.speaker: Yuyun Wahyuningrum
insights.so_what: The resistance coalition is institutionalising around state-level actors, a signal of how a post-war settlement could be structured.

insights.claim: Veteran leaders in groups like the Karen National Union remain committed to federalism, while younger activists and diaspora communities increasingly question whether conventional federalism offers enough autonomy after decades of broken agreements and failed peace processes.
insights.speaker: Yuyun Wahyuningrum
insights.so_what: Generational turnover could push resistance demands toward looser, more confederal arrangements, complicating negotiations.

insights.claim: A Myanmar settlement will likely need a flexible arrangement combining different degrees of autonomy, stronger state-level authority and negotiated power sharing between the union and self-governing territories, rather than a single model imposed from the capital.
insights.speaker: Yuyun Wahyuningrum
insights.so_what: Expect asymmetric, negotiated outcomes in which territorial actors retain significant powers.

insights.claim: Confederation's greatest weakness for Myanmar could be the autonomy that makes it attractive: constituent territories could become so self-reliant that cooperation on national issues becomes difficult, and a weak centre could struggle to decide when constituent governments disagree.
insights.speaker: Yuyun Wahyuningrum
insights.so_what: A confederal outcome may produce fragmentation and policy paralysis rather than stability.

insights.claim: Resource-rich areas of Myanmar controlling jade, hydropower or major trade routes might resist fiscal redistribution under a confederal model, deepening regional inequalities.
insights.speaker: Yuyun Wahyuningrum
insights.so_what: Control of jade, hydropower and trade corridors will be the core bargaining chips — and the likely flashpoints — in any revenue-sharing settlement.

insights.claim: Greater autonomy does not automatically mean greater inclusion; in Rakhine a settlement must address not only Rakhine's relationship with the union but also the rights and political participation of minorities including the Rohingya.
insights.speaker: Yuyun Wahyuningrum
insights.so_what: Decentralisation without rights protections could shift exclusion from national to local level, sustaining atrocity and displacement risk.
insights.quote: Decentralisation without strong rights protections could simply move exclusion from the national level to the local one.

insights.claim: ASEAN has approached Myanmar mainly through the sovereign state and the Five-Point Consensus, but if authority is dispersed among ethnic administrations and resistance territories, Naypyidaw-centred diplomacy risks overlooking realities on the ground.
insights.speaker: Yuyun Wahyuningrum
insights.so_what: Regional diplomacy that engages only the junta is unlikely to influence the actors who actually control territory.
insights.quote: diplomacy centred only on Naypyidaw risks overlooking important political realities on the ground.

insights.claim: ASEAN should broaden engagement beyond the military and the National Unity Government to ethnic political organisations, resistance actors, women, youth and civil society, without this implying recognition of new states or endorsement of territorial claims.
insights.speaker: Yuyun Wahyuningrum
insights.so_what: Offers a template for engaging de facto authorities while avoiding formal recognition issues.

insights.claim: The core challenge in Myanmar is not redistributing power from the centre but sharing the power that has already emerged across the country among actors who acquired territory and built institutions during five years of war.
insights.speaker: Yuyun Wahyuningrum
insights.so_what: Reframes peace-process expectations: holders of territorial power will negotiate from strength, not as supplicants.
